pages.title: Foundations
pages.description: This section provides an overview of the major issues in research and in evaluation. This is probably the best place for you to begin learning about research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Language Of Research
pages.description: We'll start by considering five really big multi-syllable words that researchers sometimes use to describe what they do.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Five Big Words
pages.description: Here, I want to introduce you to five terms that I think help to describe some of the key aspects of contemporary social research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types of Questions
pages.description: There are three basic types of questions that research projects can address: Descriptive, Relational, & Casual.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Time in Research
pages.description: I want to introduce one of the most fundamental distinctions in research design nomenclature: cross-sectional versus longitudinal studies.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types of Relationships
pages.description: Relationships between variables can be correlational and causal in nature, and may have different patterns (none, positive, negative, inverse, etc.)
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Variables
pages.description: A variable is any entity that can take on different values, e.g. age, country. A dependent variable is one which is affected by another (independent) variable.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Hypotheses
pages.description: An hypothesis is a specific statement predicting what you expect will happen in your study in concrete terms. Exploratory studies do not require hypotheses.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types of Data
pages.description: Here, I want to make a fundamental distinction between two types of data: qualitative and quantitative.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Unit of Analysis
pages.description: The unit of analysis is the major entity that you are analysing in your study, e.g. if comparing classroom test scores, the unit of analysis is each child.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Two Research Fallacies
pages.description: A fallacy is an error in reasoning, usually based on mistaken assumptions.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Philosophy of Research
pages.description: All research is based on assumptions about how the world is perceived and how we can best come to understand it.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Structure of Research
pages.description: Most research projects share same general structure: starting with a broad area of interest, narrowing the question down, address the original broad question.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Deduction & Induction
pages.description: Deduction (top-down) & Induction (bottom-up) are the two broad methods of reasoning used in logic. Induction is more exploratory than the narrower deduction.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Positivism & Post-Positivism
pages.description: The purpose of science is simply to stick to what we can observe and measure. Knowledge of anything beyond that, a positivist would hold, is impossible.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Introduction to Validity
pages.description: Validity: the best available approximation to the truth of a given proposition, inference, or conclusion.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Ethics in Research
pages.description: We are going through a time of profound change in our understanding of the ethics of applied social research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Conceptualizing
pages.description: One of the most difficult aspects of research -- and one of the least discussed -- is how to develop the idea for the research project in the first place.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Problem Formulation
pages.description: Probably one of the most common sources of research ideas is the experience of practical problems in the field.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Concept Mapping
pages.description: Concept mapping is a general method that can be used to help any individual or group to describe their ideas about some topic in a pictorial form.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Evaluation Research
pages.description: The Introduction to Evaluation Research presents an overview of what evaluation is and how it differs from social research generally.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Introduction to Evaluation
pages.description: Evaluation is a methodological area that is closely related to, but distinguishable from more traditional social research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The Planning-Evaluation Cycle
pages.description: Often, evaluation is construed as part of a larger managerial or administrative process. Sometimes this is referred to as the planning-evaluation cycle.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: An Evaluation Culture
pages.description: What would an evaluation culture look like? What should its values be?
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Sampling
pages.description: Sampling is the process of selecting units (e.g. people, organizations) from a population of interest to generalize the results back to the chosen population.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: External Validity
pages.description: External validity is the degree to which the conclusions in your study would hold for other persons in other places and at other times, based upon generalizing.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Sampling Terminology
pages.description: The major question that motivates sampling in the first place is: "Who do you want to generalize to?" Or should it be: "To whom do you want to generalize?"
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Statistical Terms in Sampling
pages.description: When we sample, the units that we sample -- usually people -- supply us with one or more responses.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Probability Sampling
pages.description: Probability sampling is any method of sampling that utilizes some form of random selection, e.g. Simple Random Sampling, Systematic Random Sampling etc.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Nonprobability Sampling
pages.description: Nonprobability sampling is used in social research when random sampling is not feasible and is broadly split into accidental or purposive sampling categories.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Measurement
pages.description: Measurement is the process of observing and recording the observations that are collected as part of a research effort, e.g. Surveys, Scaling & Qualitative.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Construct Validity
pages.description: Definition. Construct validity: The degree to which inferences can be made from a study's operationalizations to the theoretical constructs they were based on.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Measurement Validity Types
pages.description: Types of validity that are typically mentioned when talking about the quality of measurement: Face, Content, Predictive  Concurrent, Convergent & Discriminant.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Idea of Construct Validity
pages.description: Construct validity is an assessment of how well you translated your ideas or theories into actual programs or measures.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Convergent & Discriminant Validity
pages.description: Convergent and discriminant validity are subtypes of construct validity. Demonstrating evidence of both also demonstrates evidence for construct validity.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Threats to Construct Validity
pages.description: Before we launch into a discussion of the most common threats to construct validity, let's recall what a threat to validity is.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The Nomological Network
pages.description: The nomological network is an idea that was developed by Lee Cronbach and Paul Meehl in 1955 (Cronbach, L. and Meehl, P. (1955).
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The Multitrait-Multimethod Matrix
pages.description: The Multitrait-Multimethod Matrix (hereafter labeled MTMM) is an approach to assessing the construct validity of a set of measures in a study.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Pattern Matching for Construct Validity
pages.description: Pattern matching always involves an attempt to link two patterns where one is a theoretical pattern and the other is an observed or operational one.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Reliability
pages.description: Reliability has to do with the quality of measurement. In its everyday sense, reliability is the "consistency" or "repeatability" of your measures.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: True Score Theory
pages.description: True Score Theory is a theory about measurement. Like all theories, you need to recognize that it is not proven.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Measurement Error
pages.description: Here, we'll look at the differences between these two types of errors and try to diagnose their effects on our research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Theory of Reliability
pages.description: What is reliability? We hear the term used a lot in research contexts, but what does it really mean?
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types of Reliability
pages.description: There are 4 general classes of reliability estimates, each with pros & cons; Inter-Rater or Inter-Observer, Test-Retest, Parallel-Forms & Internal Consistency.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Reliability & Validity
pages.description: We often think of reliability and validity as separate ideas but, in fact, they're related to each other.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Levels of Measurement
pages.description: The levels of measurement (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, & Ratio) outline the relationship between the values that are assigned to the attributes for a variable.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Survey Research
pages.description: Survey research is a crucial area of measurement in applied social research. You must consider a survey's type, methodology, and construction to ensure success.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types of Surveys
pages.description: Survey research is one of the most important areas of measurement in applied social research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Selecting the Survey Method
pages.description: Selecting the type of survey you are going to use is one of the most critical decisions in many social research contexts.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Constructing the Survey
pages.description: Constructing a survey instrument is an art in itself. There are numerous small decisions that must be made  about content, wording, format, placement.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types Of Questions
pages.description: Survey questions can be divided into two broad types: structured and unstructured.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Question Content
pages.description: For each question in your survey, you should ask yourself how well it addresses the content you are trying to get at.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Response Format
pages.description: The response format is how you collect the answer from the respondent.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Question Wording
pages.description: One of the major difficulties in writing good survey questions is getting the wording right.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Question Placement
pages.description: One of the most difficult tasks facing the survey designer involves the ordering of questions.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Interviews
pages.description: Interviews are among the most challenging and rewarding forms of measurement.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Plus & Minus of Survey Methods
pages.description: It's hard to compare the advantages and disadvantages of the major different survey types.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Scaling
pages.description: Scaling is the branch of measurement that involves the construction of an instrument that associates qualitative constructs with quantitative metric units.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: General Issues in Scaling
pages.description: S.S. Stevens came up with what I think is most straightforward definition of scaling; Scaling is the assignment of objects to numbers according to a rule.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Thurstone Scaling
pages.description: Thurstone was one of the first and most productive scaling theorists. He actually invented three different methods for developing a unidimensional scale.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Likert Scaling
pages.description: Like Thurstone or Guttman Scaling, Likert Scaling is a unidimensional scaling method.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Guttman Scaling
pages.description: Guttman scaling is also sometimes known as cumulative scaling or scalogram analysis.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Qualitative Measures
pages.description: Qualitative research is a vast and complex area of methodology that can easily take up whole textbooks on its own.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The Qualitative Debate
pages.description: There has probably been the most energy expended on debating the differences between and relative advantages of qualitative and quantitative methods.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Qualitative Data
pages.description: Qualitative data is any information captured in social research that is not numerical in nature, e.g. Interviews, Direct Observation, Written Documents.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Qualitative Approaches
pages.description: A qualitative "approach" is a general way of thinking about conducting qualitative research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Qualitative Methods
pages.description: There are a wide variety of methods that are common in qualitative measurement. Here I discuss a few of the more common methods.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Qualitative Validity
pages.description: Some qualitative researchers reject the framework of validity that is commonly accepted in more quantitative research in the social sciences.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Unobtrusive Measures
pages.description: Unobtrusive measures don't require the researcher to intrude in the research context, e.g. Indirect Measures, Content Analysis, and Secondary Analysis.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Design
pages.description: A design is used to structure the research to show how all of the major parts of it work together to address the central research questions.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Internal Validity
pages.description: Internal validity means there's evidence that your study's design reflects what is observed; it's crucial to studies that try to establish causal relationships.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Establishing Cause & Effect
pages.description: How do we establish a cause-effect (causal) relationship? What criteria do we have to meet?
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Single Group Threats
pages.description: Let's consider two single group designs and then consider the threats that are most relevant with respect to internal validity.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Regression to the Mean
pages.description: A regression threat is a statistical phenomenon that occurs when a nonrandom sample from a population and two measures are imperfectly correlated.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Multiple Group Threats
pages.description: A multiple-group design typically involves at least two groups and before-after measurement.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Social Interaction Threats
pages.description: Applied social research is a human activity. And, the results of such research are affected by the human interactions involved.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Introduction to Design
pages.description: Research design can be thought of as the structure of research — it is the "glue" that holds all of the elements in a research project together.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Types of Designs
pages.description: What are the different major types of research designs? We can classify designs into a simple threefold classification by asking some key questions.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Experimental Design
pages.description: Experimental designs are often touted as the most rigorous of all research designs or, as the gold standard against which all other designs are judged.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Two-Group Experimental Designs
pages.description: The simplest of all experimental designs is the two-group posttest-only randomized experiment.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Probabilistic Equivalence
pages.description: What do I mean by the term probabilistic equivalence? Well, to begin with, I certainly don't mean that two groups are equal to each other.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Random Selection & Assignment
pages.description: Random selection is how you draw the sample of people for your study from a population. Random assignment is how you assign the sample to different groups.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Classifying Experimental Designs
pages.description: Although there are a great variety of experimental design variations, we can classify and organize them using a simple signal-to-noise ratio metaphor.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Factorial Designs
pages.description: Factorial design is used to examine treatment variations and can combine a series of independent studies into one, for efficiency. This example explores how.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Factorial Design Variations
pages.description: Here, we'll look at a number of different factorial designs. We'll begin with a two-factor design where one of the factors has more than two levels.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Randomized Block Designs
pages.description: The Randomized Block Design is research design's equivalent to stratified random sampling.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Covariance Designs
pages.description: The basic Analysis of Covariance Design (ANCOVA or ANACOVA) is a just pretest-posttest randomized experimental design.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Hybrid Experimental Designs
pages.description: Hybrid experimental designs are just what the name implies ⁠— new strains that are formed by combining features of more established designs.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Quasi-Experimental Design
pages.description: A quasi-experimental design looks somewhat like an experimental design but lacks the random assignment element. Nonequivalent groups design is a common form.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The Nonequivalent Groups Design
pages.description: The Non-Equivalent Groups Design (hereafter NEGD) is probably the most frequently used design in social research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The Regression-Discontinuity Design
pages.description: The Regression-Discontinuity design is seen as a useful method for determining whether a program or treatment is effective.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Other Quasi-Experimental Designs
pages.description: Here, I'll briefly present a number of the more interesting or important quasi-experimental designs.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Relationships Among Pre-Post Designs
pages.description: There are 3 main types of pre-post program-comparison group designs: Randomized Experimental (RE), Nonequivalent Group (NEGD) & Regression-Discontinuity (RD).
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Designing Designs for Research
pages.description: Learn the basic principles of good design logic; minimising threats to validity, design construction, expansion, strategy and structure, and hybrid design.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Advances in Quasi-Experimentation
pages.description: Perspectives on quasi-experimentations over time are advancing with the underlying theme of human judgement driving a more scientific outlook on the topic.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Analysis
pages.description: By the time you get to the analysis of your data, most of the really difficult work has been done. It's much more difficult to define the research problem.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Conclusion Validity
pages.description: Of the four types of validity, conclusion validity is undoubtedly the least considered and most misunderstood.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Threats to Conclusion Validity
pages.description: A threat to conclusion validity is a factor that can lead you to reach an incorrect conclusion about a relationship in your observations.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Improving Conclusion Validity
pages.description: Here are some general guidelines you can follow in designing your study that will help improve conclusion validity.
pages.author: Conjointly

pages.title: Statistical Power
pages.description: There are four interrelated components that influence the conclusions you might reach from a statistical test in a research project.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Data Preparation
pages.description: Data Preparation involves checking or logging the data in; checking the data for accuracy; entering the data into the computer; transforming the data...
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Descriptive Statistics
pages.description: Descriptive statistics are used to describe the basic features of your study's data and form the basis of virtually every quantitative analysis of data.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Correlation
pages.description: A correlation describes the degree of relationship between two variables. Accurate calculation of this statistic is crucial for effective research analysis.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Inferential Statistics
pages.description: Inferential statistics in research draws conclusions that cannot be derived from descriptive statistics, i.e. to infer population opinion from sample data.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: The T-Test
pages.description: The t-test gauges whether the means of two groups are statistically different from each other using ratio: difference between group means/variability of groups.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Dummy Variables
pages.description: A dummy variable is a numerical variable used in regression analysis to represent subgroups of the sample in your study.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: General Linear Model
pages.description: The General Linear Model (GLM) underlies most of the statistical analyses that are used in applied and social research.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Posttest-Only Analysis
pages.description: To analyze the two-group posttest-only randomized experimental design we need an analysis that meets four requirements.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Factorial Design Analysis
pages.description: Here is the regression model statement for a simple 2 x 2 Factorial Design.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Randomized Block Analysis
pages.description: I've decided to present the statistical model for the Randomized Block Design in regression analysis notation.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Analysis of Covariance
pages.description: I've decided to present the statistical model for the Analysis of Covariance design in regression analysis notation.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Nonequivalent Groups Analysis
pages.description: The design notation for the Non-Equivalent Groups Design (NEGD) shows that we have a program and comparison group, and that each is measured pre and post.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Regression-Discontinuity Analysis
pages.description: The basic RD Design is a two-group pretest-posttest model as indicated in the design notation.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Regression Point Displacement Analysis
pages.description: The notation for RPD design shows that the statistical analysis requires a posttest score, pretest score & a variable to represent the treatment group.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Write-Up
pages.description: So now that you've completed the research project, what do you do? I know you won't want to hear this, but your work is still far from done.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Key Elements
pages.description: This page describes the elements or criteria that you must typically address in a research paper.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.title: Formatting
pages.description: The instructions provided here are for a research article or a research report.
pages.author: William M.K. Trochim

pages.description: This paper is provided only to give you an idea of what a research paper might look like.
